explanation:
## The program

```cpp
if (b == 0)
    std::cout << "cannot divide by zero\n";
else if (a % b == 0)
    std::cout << "divides " << a / b << "\n";
else
    std::cout << "remainder " << a % b << "\n";
```

The reference takes the zero case out first with its own branch,
which makes the `&&` unnecessary: everything after the first `if`
already knows `b` is not zero. That is usually the better shape when
the guarded case has something of its own to say. The `&&` version

```cpp
if (b != 0 && a % b == 0)       std::cout << "divides " << a / b << "\n";
else if (b != 0)                std::cout << "remainder " << a % b << "\n";
else                            std::cout << "cannot divide by zero\n";
```

is equally correct and repeats `b != 0`, which is a hint that the
test wants to be a branch of its own.

## Short-circuit evaluation

`&&` and `||` are the two operators in C++ that are specified **not**
to evaluate both sides:

```
left && right       right is evaluated only if left is true
left || right       right is evaluated only if left is false
```

That is a guarantee, not an optimisation, and there is a sequence
point between the two — the left operand is fully evaluated,
side-effects included, before the right one is even considered. So
this is a correct and idiomatic thing to write:

```cpp
if (p != nullptr && p->ready)        // dereference guarded by the test
if (i < v.size() && v[i] == x)       // index guarded by the test
if (b != 0 && a % b == 0)            // division guarded by the test
```

and each one is broken by swapping the operands. The guard has to be
on the left, because "left first" is the only ordering the language
promises.

## `&` is not a short `&&`

`a & b` is bitwise AND. It evaluates both operands always, and on
`bool`s it gives the right answer for the wrong reason — so
`b != 0 & a % b == 0` divides by zero after all. It also has lower
precedence than `==`, so that line does not even parse the way it
reads. Two different operators with similar spellings and different
rules; use `&&` for logic.

## Why division by zero is not an exception

Integer division by zero in C++ is undefined behaviour. Not an
exception to catch, not a value to check afterwards — the standard
declines to say what the program does at all. On most hardware it
traps and the process dies, which feels like an error being
reported, but you cannot rely on it: with optimisation on, a
compiler may reason backwards from "this division happens" to "`b`
is not zero" and delete a later test you wrote. The guard must come
first.

Floating point is different. `1.0 / 0.0` is `inf` under IEEE 754 and
is perfectly well defined, which is why the same mistake in `double`
arithmetic produces a strange number instead of a crash.

## What this does not check

The one input where the division itself is undefined even with a
non-zero divisor: the most negative `int` divided by -1, whose true
quotient has no representation. The constraints keep the numbers
small enough that it cannot arise here, and a program handling
arbitrary input would have to test for it by name.
